specPoints.text: know and use the relationship between the speed, frequency and wavelength of a wave: wave speed = frequency × wavelength
use the relationship between frequency and time period: frequency = 1 / time period
use the above relationships in different contexts including sound waves and electromagnetic waves

primer.text: You can already define wave speed, frequency and wavelength, and you know every wave obeys the same rhythm. One small equation now ties those three together, and a second links frequency with the time period. With them you can work wave questions for ripples, sound and light alike, which is exactly what this lesson trains.

lessons.title: The wave speed equation
sourceHeadings: Formula triangle for the wave speed equation
lessons.opening: Every wave, from a stadium ripple to a gamma ray, obeys one speed law: wave speed equals frequency multiplied by wavelength. In symbols, v = f x lambda, with v in metres per second, f in hertz and lambda in metres. A formula triangle makes rearranging it a covering exercise rather than algebra.
keyPoints: All waves obey the wave speed equation v = f x lambda.
v is the wave speed in metres per second.
f is the frequency in hertz and lambda the wavelength in metres.
A formula triangle covers the quantity you want to find and reads off the arrangement of the other two.

low.restatement: The speed of a wave is its frequency times its wavelength, so fast waves are either repeating quickly or stretching far per cycle.
low.analogy: Steps per second times stride length gives walking speed; frequency is the steps and wavelength is the stride.
low.examPointer: Write the equation first, then substitute: the equation line itself usually scores a mark.

medium.restatement: Because v = f x lambda holds for every wave, changing the medium changes speed and wavelength together while the source keeps the frequency fixed, a consistency examiners like to probe.
medium.analogy: Marching soldiers entering mud: the pace (frequency) stays set by the drummer while the stride (wavelength) shortens and the column slows.
medium.examPointer: Keep unit discipline: hertz times metres gives metres per second; mismatched units are the classic lost mark.

check.stem: The wave speed equation in symbols is:

options.explanation: Dividing would give the wrong dimensions; the law multiplies.
Wave speed equals frequency multiplied by wavelength.
That would divide a length by a count per second.
Rearranged wrongly: frequency is v divided by lambda.

check.stem: In v = f x lambda, the quantity v stands for:

options.explanation: Volume has no role in the wave equation.
Voltage belongs to electricity, not this law.

options.text: wave speed in metres per second
options.explanation: v carries the speed in m/s.
Frequency is the f term.

check.stem: A wave has frequency 2 Hz and wavelength 0.5 m. Its speed is:

options.explanation: That comes from multiplying 0.5 by 0.5; the frequency is 2.
Adding instead of multiplying is not the law.
That divides by the wavelength instead of multiplying.

check.stem: Rearranging v = f x lambda to find the wavelength gives:

options.explanation: Dividing speed by frequency leaves the wavelength.
That inverts the rearrangement.
Multiplying both quantities gives speed squared units.
The law multiplies, so the inverse divides.

check.stem: A sound wave has speed 300 m/s and frequency 500 Hz. Its wavelength is:

options.explanation: That multiplies instead of dividing; a wavelength of 150 km is not physical here.
Adding speed and frequency has no meaning in this law.
That divides frequency by speed, the inverted ratio.

check.stem: State the wave speed equation in words and in symbols.
check.modelAnswer: Wave speed = frequency x wavelength, written v = f x lambda.

check.stem: State the units of v, f and lambda in the wave speed equation.
check.modelAnswer: v is in metres per second, f in hertz and lambda in metres.

check.stem: Explain how the formula triangle is used to find frequency from speed and wavelength.
check.modelAnswer: Covering f in the triangle leaves v over lambda, so frequency is the wave speed divided by the wavelength, which is the rearrangement of v = f x lambda for f.

check.stem: A water ripple travels at 0.4 m/s with wavelength 0.1 m. Calculate its frequency, showing the equation you use.
check.modelAnswer: f = v / lambda = 0.4 / 0.1 = 4 Hz, using the wave speed equation rearranged for frequency.

lessons.title: Frequency & time period
lessons.opening: Frequency and time period are two views of one rhythm, and the equation f = 1 / T converts between them. Divide one second by the period and you have the count of waves per second; turn the frequency upside down and you have the seconds per wave. The worked example puts the sums to work on light itself.
keyPoints: The relationship is frequency = 1 / time period, written f = 1 / T.
f is measured in hertz and T in seconds.
Turning the period upside down gives the frequency, and the reverse rearrangement gives T = 1 / f.
A wave repeating every 0.02 s has frequency 50 Hz by the relationship.

low.restatement: Frequency and period are reciprocals: more waves per second means fewer seconds per wave.
low.analogy: A bakery that finishes one loaf every 0.5 minutes makes 2 loaves per minute; the rate and the per-item time are inverses.
low.examPointer: Quote f = 1 / T before substituting; the stated relationship is usually worth a mark on its own.

medium.restatement: The reciprocal law lets exam questions hop between the time picture and the count picture: a short period means a high frequency, which for a fixed wave speed means a short wavelength through v = f x lambda.
medium.analogy: Heart monitors show both beats per minute and the gap between beats; the two numbers carry the same information flipped.
medium.examPointer: Keep periods in seconds, not milliseconds, before substituting; unit slips here are the most common error.

check.stem: The equation linking frequency and time period is:

options.explanation: They are reciprocal, not equal.
Frequency is the reciprocal of the period.
No squaring appears in the relationship.
That just restates the period as frequency.

check.stem: A wave has time period 0.5 s. Its frequency is:

options.explanation: That restates the period as a frequency.
No factor of ten is involved.
Nothing adds one here.

check.stem: A wave repeats every 0.02 s. Its frequency is:

options.explanation: That is the period quoted as a frequency.
That drops a zero in the division.
That inserts an extra factor of ten.

check.stem: Rearranging f = 1 / T for the period gives:

options.explanation: Period and frequency are not equal.
The relationship is division, not subtraction.
The reciprocal swaps sides symmetrically.
That restates frequency as the period.

check.stem: A signal has frequency 200 Hz. Its time period is:

options.explanation: That restates the frequency as a period in seconds.
That would follow from a frequency of 5 Hz.
No scaling by ten applies.

check.stem: State in words how frequency and the time period are related.
check.modelAnswer: Frequency equals one divided by the time period.

check.stem: State the unit of time period and the unit of frequency.
check.modelAnswer: Time period is measured in seconds and frequency in hertz.

check.stem: Explain why a wave with a shorter time period has a higher frequency.
check.modelAnswer: Frequency counts the waves arriving each second by dividing one second by the time each wave takes, so shrinking the per-wave time raises the per-second count.

check.stem: A vibrating toy completes 200 vibrations per second. Calculate the time period of one vibration.
check.modelAnswer: T = 1 / f = 1 / 200 = 0.005 s, using the reciprocal relationship rearranged for the period.

lessons.title: Using the relationships in different contexts
lessons.opening: The two relationships are not tied to any one wave type: sound in air, ripples on water and light in space all answer to v = f x lambda and f = 1 / T. Exam questions simply dress the same algebra in different contexts, so the skill is spotting which quantity each sentence hands you and converting units first.
keyPoints: The wave equation applies to every type of wave, including sound and electromagnetic waves.
Frequency given in kHz must be converted to hertz before substitution.
Wavelengths given in centimetres can be worked in centimetres per second if units are kept consistent.
Use lambda for wavelength and state word equations if symbols are forgotten.

low.restatement: Whichever wave a question describes, the same two equations answer it; only the numbers and units change.
low.analogy: One recipe bakes a cake, cookies or a loaf: same method, different ingredients.
low.examPointer: Convert kHz to Hz before any substitution; 1 kHz = 1000 Hz is quoted in the notes as the slip to avoid.

medium.restatement: Context questions chain the two relationships: a period gives a frequency through the reciprocal law, and that frequency with a speed gives a wavelength, or the reverse chain recovers a speed from a count and a length.
medium.analogy: Two gears in a gearbox: turning either one eventually turns the other, whichever the question hands you first.
medium.examPointer: State the units in the final answer; a bare number for a speed loses the unit mark even when the arithmetic is right.

check.stem: The wave speed equation can be applied to:

options.explanation: The law is not restricted to mechanical waves.
The law is not restricted to electromagnetic waves.
Any single-wave-type reading is too narrow.

options.text: all waves, including sound and electromagnetic waves
options.explanation: The relationship is universal across wave types.

check.stem: A frequency of 200 kHz expressed in hertz is:

options.explanation: 1 kHz = 1000 Hz, so 200 kHz = 200000 Hz.
That drops the kilo- prefix conversion.
That multiplies by an extra thousand.
That divides instead of multiplying.

check.stem: A radio station broadcasts at 200 kHz with wavelength 1500 m. The wave speed is:

options.explanation: That drops two zeros from the product.
That divides the frequency by the wavelength.
That loses a factor of a hundred.

check.stem: A sound wave moves at 330 m/s with time period 0.0001 s. Its frequency is:

options.explanation: That quotes the period as the frequency.
That drops a zero in the division.
The speed does not set the frequency on its own.

check.stem: That same sound wave (330 m/s, frequency 10000 Hz) has wavelength:

options.explanation: That divides by 100 instead of 10000.
That is off by three orders of magnitude.
That multiplies instead of dividing.

check.stem: State the conversion between kilohertz and hertz.
State the two equations a wave-context calculation may need.
check.modelAnswer: v = f x lambda and f = 1 / T, with T = 1 / f as the reverse form.

check.stem: Explain why units are converted before substituting into the wave equation.
check.modelAnswer: The equation only balances when speed is in metres per second, frequency in hertz and wavelength in metres, so mixed units like kHz or centimetres would produce answers that are wrong by factors of a thousand or a hundred.

check.stem: A hammer strikes steel rail every 2.0 ms. Given the vibration wave travels the rail at 6000 m/s, calculate the wavelength along the rail.
check.modelAnswer: Period 2.0 ms = 0.002 s gives f = 1 / 0.002 = 500 Hz; then lambda = v / f = 6000 / 500 = 12 m.

glossary.definition: The distance a wave pattern travels each second, measured in metres per second.
A covering trick for rearranging a three-quantity equation of the form a = b x c.
Kilohertz; one kilohertz is one thousand hertz.

workedExample.prompt: Visible light has a frequency of about 6 x 10^14 Hz. How long does it take for one complete cycle of visible light to enter our eyes?
steps: List the known value: frequency f = 6 x 10^14 Hz.
Time and frequency are linked through the period, so state T = 1 / f.
Substitute and calculate: T = 1 / (6 x 10^14) = 1.67 x 10^-15 s (to 2 decimal places).
workedExample.finalAnswer: One complete cycle of visible light takes about 1.67 x 10^-15 s.
